Ptolemy entered Antioch and put on the crown of Asia. He placed two crowns on his head, from Asia to Egypt.
King Alexander was in Cilicia at that time, because the inhabitants of that country had rebelled against him.
When Alexander heard this, he came against him in battle. Ptolemy marched out against him with a large army and great force, and defeated Alexander.
Alexander fled to Arabia to hide there, while King Ptolemy rose to power.
Zabdiel the Arab took Alexander's head and sent it to Ptolemy.
King Ptolemy himself also died three days later. Some of those he had left in the fortresses died in those very fortresses.
Demetrius became king in the year one hundred and sixty-seven.
In those days Jonathan gathered an army from Judea to fight against the inhabitants of the citadel in Jerusalem, and he constructed many siege engines against it.
Some men who were hated by their own people, wicked men, went to the king and told him, “Look, Jonathan is encamped [?] against the citadel.”
When the king heard this, he became angry. As soon as he heard it, he set out and came to Ptolemais. He wrote to Jonathan not to build the citadel, but to go and meet him quickly at Ptolemais.
When Jonathan heard this, he ordered the building of the citadel to continue. He chose some of the priests and elders of Israel and put himself in danger.
He took gold, silver, vessels, and various other gifts, and went to the king at Ptolemais. He found favor with him.
Wicked men from among the people were bringing accusations against him.
The king treated him as his predecessor had treated him and honored him before all his friends.
He granted him the priesthood and all the honor he had previously enjoyed. He promoted him and made him one of his great and honored friends.
Jonathan persuaded the king to exempt Judea from paying tribute, along with the three districts of the region and Samaria. He promised him three hundred talents.
The king agreed and wrote Jonathan letters concerning everything he had requested. They read as follows:
“King Demetrius to Jonathan, my brother, and to the Jewish people: Greetings.
We have also written to you a copy of the letter we wrote to Lasthenes, our kinsman, concerning you, so that you too may know.
‘King Demetrius to Lasthenes, my father: Greetings.
We wish to show kindness to the Jewish people, our friends who maintain peaceful relations with us, because of their goodwill toward us.

We have confirmed and granted to them the territory of Judea and the three districts of Ephraim, Lydda, and Ramathaim, which were added to Judea from Samaria, together with everything under their jurisdiction, for the offerings in Jerusalem, in place of the royal revenues formerly collected from them from the crops of the land and the fruit of the trees.
Everything else that was due to us from tithes, customs duties, salt pans, and crown dues is remitted to them.
Not one of these provisions is to be revoked from now on.
Now take care to write a copy of these provisions and give it to Jonathan. Let it be displayed in a prominent, visible place on the holy mountain.’”

King Demetrius saw that the land was quiet and at peace under his rule, and that no one was opposing him. He dismissed his entire army, each man to his own home, except for those he had recruited from the islands of the nations. Then all the troops who had served his ancestors became hostile to him.
Trypho had formerly belonged to Alexander’s household. He saw that the whole army was grumbling against Demetrius, so he went to Malchus the Arab, who was raising Antiochus, Alexander’s son.

He asked him to hand the boy over to him so that he could make him king in his father’s place. He told him everything Demetrius had done and how his army had become hostile to him. He stayed there for many days.
Jonathan sent word to King Demetrius to remove the occupants of the citadel from Jerusalem, as well as the occupants of the fortresses, for they were fighting against Israel.
Demetrius sent word to Jonathan, saying, “I will not only do these things for you and your people, but I will also bestow great honor on you and your people when I have the opportunity.
But now you would do well to send me men to help me, because my entire army has deserted me.”
Jonathan sent three thousand valiant men to Antioch. They came to the king, and the king was glad at their arrival.
All the inhabitants of the city, about one hundred and twenty thousand, gathered in the center of the city. They wanted to kill King Demetrius.
The king fled and went into the palace. The townspeople seized all the exits from the city and began fighting.
The king called on the Jews to help him, and they all gathered around him together. They spread throughout the city and killed about one hundred thousand people in the city that day.
They burned the city, took a great deal of plunder that day, and rescued the king.
The inhabitants of the city saw that the Jews had grown strong and had taken control of the whole city as they wished. They lost heart and cried out to the king, pleading with him and saying,
“Give us your pledge, and let the Jews stop fighting against us and the city.”

They laid down their weapons, gave their right hands in pledge, and made peace. The Jews were greatly honored before the king and throughout his kingdom, and they returned to Jerusalem with a great deal of plunder.
King Demetrius sat on his royal throne, and the land became quiet and peaceful under him.
But he proved false in everything he had said. He changed his attitude toward Jonathan and did not give him everything he had promised him, but instead oppressed him severely.
After this, Tryphon returned with the young boy Antiochus, who became king and put on the crown.
All the troops that Demetrius had dispersed gathered around him. He fought against Demetrius, and Demetrius was defeated and fled.
Tryphon took all his animals and captured Antioch.
The young Antiochus wrote to Jonathan, saying, “I confirm you in the high priesthood, give you authority over all four districts, and appoint you as one of the king’s Friends.”
He sent him gold vessels and tableware, and gave him permission to drink from gold vessels, wear purple, and wear a gold clasp on his garments.
He appointed his brother Simon governor from the borders of Tyre to the border of Egypt.

Jonathan set out and traveled through the regions beyond the river and through the cities. All the troops of Syria gathered around him to help him. Jonathan came to Ashkelon, and the inhabitants of the city welcomed him with great acclaim.
He went from there to Gaza, but the people of Gaza shut him out. He besieged it, burned all its surrounding areas, and plundered them.

The people of Gaza pleaded with Jonathan, and he gave them his pledge. He took the sons of their leading men as hostages and sent them to Jerusalem. Then he traveled through the land as far as Damascus.
Jonathan heard that Demetrius’s commanders had come to Kedesh in Galilee with a large army, intending to remove him from office.
He went to meet them, but left his brother Simon in the country.
Simon besieged Beth-zur and fought against it for many days, keeping its inhabitants shut in.
They asked him to give them his pledge, and he gave it to them. He brought them out of there, captured the city, and stationed a garrison in it.
Jonathan and his army camped by the waters of Gennesaret. Early in the morning they went to the plain of Hazor.
There the army of the Philistines met him on the plain, and they sent men to lie in ambush against him.
The men rose from behind them and began to fight, and all Jonathan’s men fled.
None of them remained with him except Mattathias son of Absalom and Judas son of Haphai, senior commanders of the army.
Jonathan tore his clothes, put dust on his head, and prayed.
He turned against them in battle and defeated them, and they fled.
When those who had been with him saw the enemy fleeing, they turned back and came to him. They pursued them as far as [?], their camp, and camped there.
About three thousand Philistine men fell that day, and Jonathan returned to Jerusalem.
Jonathan saw that the time was favorable to him, so he chose men and sent them to Rome to confirm and renew their friendship with the Romans.
He also sent letters to the Spartans and to other places in the same way.
They went to Rome, entered their senate house, and said to them, “Jonathan the high priest and the Jewish people have sent us to renew the friendship and alliance as before.”
The Romans welcomed them gladly and gave them letters so that, in every territory they passed through, they would be sent safely on their way to the land of Judah.
This is a copy of the letter Jonathan sent to the Spartans:
Jonathan the high priest, the elders, the priests, and all the Jewish people, to our brothers the Spartans: greetings.
“For even now letters have been sent to Onias the high priest from Darius your king, stating that you are our brothers, as the letters show.
Onias had received with honor the man who had been sent, and had accepted these letters written concerning alliance and friendship.
We, however, do not rely on these things, because we have for our encouragement the holy books that are in our hands.
For this reason we wished to send to you to renew our friendship and brotherhood with you, so that we would not become strangers to you. For a long time has passed since you sent word to us.
We always remember you without fail, at the festivals and on the appointed days, in all the offerings we present and in all our prayers, as it is necessary and right to remember one's brothers.
We rejoice greatly in your glory.
But many troubles have surrounded us, and all the kings around us have waged great wars against us.
We did not wish to trouble you or the rest of our friends and allies in all our wars.
For we have help from heaven, which helps us, rescues us from our enemies, and humbles them before us.
We chose Numenius son of Antiochus and Antipater son of Jason and sent them to the Romans to renew our alliance and friendship with them.
We instructed them to come to you as well, to ask about your welfare, and to give you our letters concerning the renewal of our brotherhood with you.
Now you will do well to write us copies of these things.”
This is a copy of the letter he had sent:
“Aniris, king of the Spartans, to Onias the great high priest: Greetings.
It has been found in a written document concerning the Spartans and the Jews that they are brothers and are descended from Abraham.
Now that we have learned these things, you will do well to write to us about your welfare.
We are writing to you about everything concerning us, because everything you have is ours, and everything we have is yours. We have instructed them to tell you all these things.”
Jonathan heard that the commanders of Demetrius's forces had returned with an army larger than the first to wage war against him.
Jonathan set out from Jerusalem and met them in the land of Hamath, for he would not give them an opportunity to trample through his land.
He sent spies to their camp. They returned and told him, “They are planning to attack you during the night.”
When the sun set, Jonathan ordered those with him to stay awake, have their weapons ready, and be prepared for battle throughout the night. He also stationed guards outside the camp all around it.
Their enemies heard that Jonathan and those with him were ready for battle. They were afraid and trembled in their hearts, and they left fires burning in their camps and fled.
But Jonathan and those with him did not know until morning, for they could see the fires burning.
Jonathan pursued them but did not catch them, for they had crossed the river called Eleutherus.
Jonathan turned against the Arabs called the Zabadeans, defeated them, and took their plunder.
He set out and came to Damascus, passing through the territories.
Simon went out and traveled as far as Ashkelon and the fortresses around it. Then he turned toward Joppa and captured it.
For he heard that they wanted to surrender the fortress to Demetrius's supporters, and he stationed a garrison there to guard it.
Jonathan returned, gathered the elders of the people, and consulted with them about building fortresses in Judea

and raising the walls of Jerusalem higher. They built a high embankment between the citadel and the city so that it would be separated from the city and the city would be independent, with no buying or selling between them.
They gathered to rebuild the city. Part of the wall beside the ravine on the east had fallen, and he filled in the place called Chaphenatha.
Simon built up Adida in the plain and strengthened it with gates and bars.
Trypho wanted to become king over Asia, put on the crown, and lay hands on King Antiochus.
But he was afraid that Jonathan might not allow him to do so, or might fight against him. He was looking for an opportunity to seize Jonathan and destroy him, and he set out and came to Beth-shan.
Jonathan went out with forty thousand men chosen for battle and came to Beth-shan.
Trypho saw that Jonathan had come with a large army, and he was afraid to lay hands on him.

He welcomed him with praise and honored him before all his friends. He gave him gifts and told his friends to do so, and they too gave gifts to him and his army. He ordered them to obey Jonathan as they would obey him.
He said to Jonathan, “Why have you gone to the trouble of bringing all these people when we are not at war?

Now send them away, each to his own home. Choose a few men to stay with you, and come with me to Ptolemais. I will hand it over to you, along with the remaining fortresses, the remaining troops, and all those in charge of affairs. Then I will turn back and leave, for this is why I came.”
Jonathan believed him and did as he said. He sent his army away, and it went to the land of Judea.
He kept three thousand men with him. He left two thousand of them in Galilee, while a thousand went with him.
But when Jonathan entered the city of Ptolemais, they imprisoned him there and killed with the sword everyone who had entered with him.
Trypho sent troops and cavalry to Galilee and the Great Plain to destroy all of Jonathan’s men.
They learned that Jonathan had been captured and that he and those with him had perished. They took courage, encouraged one another, and marched together, ready for battle.
Their pursuers saw that they were bitter to the depths of their souls and were fighting with all their strength, so they turned back from pursuing them.
They all arrived safely in the land of Judah. They mourned for Jonathan and those who were with him, and they were greatly afraid. All Israel mourned deeply.
All the nations around them wanted to destroy them completely, for they said, “They have no leader to help them. Now come, let us fight against them and erase their memory from among humankind.”
Simon heard that Trypho had gathered a large army to invade the land of Judea and devastate it.
He saw that the people were afraid and trembling, and he went up to Jerusalem.

He gathered the people, encouraged them, and said to them, “You know everything that I, my brothers, and my whole family have done for the law and the sanctuary, and the battles and hardships we have experienced.
For this reason all my brothers died for the sake of all Israel, and I alone am left.
Now, far be it from me to spare myself in any time of distress, for I am no better than my brothers.
Instead, I will fight for my people, our sanctuary, and our children, because all the nations have gathered to destroy us out of their hostility.”
The spirit of the people was stirred and fired up as soon as they heard his words.
They answered him loudly, “You are our leader in place of your brothers Judas and Jonathan.
Fight our battles, and we will do everything you tell us.”
Simon gathered all the fighting men and hurried to finish and complete the wall of Jerusalem, strengthening it all around.
He sent Jonathan son of Absalom to Joppa with a large army. Jonathan drove out those who were there and settled there himself.
Tryphon set out from Ptolemais with a large army to enter the land of Judah, and Jonathan was with him under guard.
Simon camped at Adida, facing the plain.
Tryphon learned that Simon had taken the place of his brother Jonathan and was ready to fight him. He sent messengers to him, saying,
“We are holding your brother Jonathan because of the money he owed the royal treasury for the affairs he administered.”
Now send one hundred talents of silver and two of his sons as hostages, lest, when he is released, he turn against us and escape from us. Then we will release him.
Simon knew that they were speaking deceitfully to him, but he sent the money and the boys, lest he cause great hostility toward Israel,
because he had not sent the money and the boys, and so they had perished.
He sent the boys and a hundred talents, but Tryphon lied and did not release Jonathan.
After this, Tryphon came to march through the land of Judah to destroy it. He went by the road to Adora, and Simon and his army went ahead of him wherever he went.
The inhabitants of the citadel sent messengers to Tryphon, asking him to come to them quickly through the wilderness and send them provisions.
Tryphon prepared all his cavalry to come that night, but there was heavy snow, and he could not come because of the snow. He set out and went to Gilead.
When Tryphon reached Baskama, he killed Jonathan, and Jonathan was buried there.
Then Tryphon turned back and went to his own land.
Simon sent for the bones of his brother Jonathan and buried him at Modein, in the city of his ancestors.
All Israel wept and mourned for him for many days.
Simon built a monument over the tomb of his father and his brothers, raising it high so that it was visible, with dressed stones carved on both sides.
He erected seven monuments, facing one another, for his father, his mother, and his four brothers.

He made elaborate structures and erected great columns for them. On the columns he carved every kind of weapon of war as an everlasting memorial. Beside the weapons he made carved ships, raising them high so that all who sailed the sea could see them.
The tomb that Simon built in Modin [?] is there to this day.
Meanwhile, Trypho dealt treacherously with Antiochus, the great king, and killed him.
He became king in his place, put on the crown of Asia, and brought great suffering upon the land.
Simon rebuilt the fortresses of Judea, surrounded them with high towers, great walls, gates, and bars, and stored provisions in the fortresses.
Simon chose men and sent them to King Demetrius to obtain relief for the land, because all Trypho’s actions had been acts of plunder.
King Demetrius sent him a reply in a letter with these words:
“King Demetrius to Simon, the high priest and friend of the king, and to the elders and the Jewish people: Greetings.
We have received the gold crown and the delegation you sent us. We are prepared to make a lasting peace with you and to write to the officials in charge of affairs to exempt you from taxes.
Everything we have written to you remains in force, and the fortresses you have built shall belong to you.
We also pardon the sins and offenses committed up to this day, and remit the crown payment you owed. Anyone who has been paying a tax in Jerusalem shall no longer pay it.
Any of your people who wish to enroll among our men may enroll, and let there be peace between us.”
In the year 170, the yoke of the nations was lifted from Israel.
The people began dating their documents and transactions: “In the first year of Simon, the great high priest, chief and leader of the Jews.”
In those days Simon laid siege to Gaza and surrounded it with an army. He made strong wooden towers and brought them up to the city wall. He battered down one tower and captured the city.
The soldiers leaped out of the wooden towers and went down into the city, and there was great turmoil within the city.
The inhabitants of the city came up with their wives and children, tearing their clothes. They cried out loudly and asked Simon to give them a pledge of peace.
They said to him, “Do not treat us according to our wickedness, but according to your kindness.”
Simon spared them and did not fight against them. He expelled them from the city and purified the houses where there had been idols. Then he entered it with praise and blessing.
He removed all impurity from it and settled there men who delighted in the law. He built a fortress in it and made a house there for himself.
Meanwhile, those living in the citadel in Jerusalem were prevented from going in and out, buying and selling. They suffered severe hunger, and many of them died of starvation.
They asked Simon to give them a pledge of peace, and he gave it to them. He expelled them from there and purified the citadel from all its impurity.

They entered the citadel on the twenty-third day of the second month in the year 171, with rejoicing, songs of praise, hosannas, lyres, and harps, because a great enemy had been crushed and removed from Israel, and the foreigner had ceased fighting against Israel.
They decreed that this day should be celebrated every year with festivity and rejoicing.
They fortified the temple hill beside the citadel, and Simon lived there with his household.
Simon saw that his son John was a mighty warrior, and he appointed him commander of all the forces. John lived in Gazara.
In the one hundred and seventy-second year, Demetrius gathered his army and went to Media to gather forces for himself and fight against Trypho.
Arsaces, king of Persia and Media, heard that Demetrius had entered his territory, and he sent one of his officials to capture him alive.
He went and attacked Demetrius’s army, captured him, brought him to Arsaces, and put him in prison.
The land was quiet and at rest throughout Simon’s lifetime. He did good things for his people, and his rule and his glory pleased them throughout his lifetime.
Along with all his glory, he took Joppa as a harbor and made an entrance for ships of the sea.
He widened and extended his people’s borders and gained possession of all their land.
He gathered many captives and took control of Gazara, Beth-zur, and the citadel. He cleared away and removed all impurity from them, and there was no one who could stand against him.
They lived and worked their land in peace. The land yielded its crops, and the trees of the land their fruit.
The elderly sat in the streets, and they all deliberated about good things. The young men were clothed in glory, not in weapons of war.
He supplied the cities with provisions and strengthened them with defensive equipment, until his glorious name became known to all the ends of the earth.
He established peace in the land, and Israel enjoyed great prosperity.
Everyone sat beneath their own vines and fig trees, and there was no one to disturb them.
Their enemies were destroyed and removed from among them, and the warriors were removed from the land. Even kings were shattered in those days.
He supported and strengthened all the poor among his people. He wiped out and removed all wickedness, injustice, and evil, and enforced the law.
He adorned the sanctuary and increased the number of vessels in the temple.
The Romans heard that Jonathan had died, and the Spartans also heard, and they were deeply distressed.
But when they heard that his brother Simon had become high priest in his place and held the land, the cities, and everything in them,
they wrote to him on a bronze tablet to renew with him the friendship and alliance they had established with his brothers Judas and Jonathan.
It was read before the assembly in Jerusalem.

This is the copy of the letter that the Spartans sent: “The rulers of the Spartans and the cities, to Simon the great high priest, to the elders, to the priests, and to the rest of the Jewish people, our brothers: Greetings.
The elders who were sent to us told us about the peace you enjoy, your honor, and your glory, and we rejoiced greatly at their arrival.
We recorded everything they said in our people’s council chamber, as follows: ‘Numenius son of Antiochus and Antipater son of Jason, elders of the Jews, came to us to renew their friendship with us.

The people were pleased to accept their friendship. They received the men with honor and placed a copy of their letters in the archives, to serve as a memorial for the Spartan people.’ They wrote to Simon the high priest with copies of these letters and their replies.
After this, Simon sent Numenius to Rome, carrying a large gold shield weighing a thousand minas, to establish an alliance with them.
When the people heard these things, they said, “What favor can we do in return for Simon the high priest and his sons?”
